cases.title: Night-time hand numbness
cases.referral: 52F, R hand numbness thumb/index/middle, wakes at night and shakes the hand. NCS R arm, r/o CTS.
cases.why: Suspected carpal tunnel syndrome needs median motor and sensory studies plus ulnar studies in the same hand, so the median results can be compared with a nerve that does not pass through the carpal tunnel.

questions.q: Taken together, what pattern do your median and ulnar results show?
options: Focal median slowing at the wrist with normal ulnar studies
Diffuse slowing in both nerves, as in a polyneuropathy
Ulnar slowing across the elbow with normal median studies
Normal studies, with the abnormal values due to a cold hand
questions.explanation: The median distal motor latency and sensory peak latency are prolonged and the median SNAP is small, while the ulnar studies in the same hand are normal and the hand was warm. That is focal median slowing at the wrist, the pattern the physician will interpret in the light of the symptoms. A polyneuropathy would affect the ulnar nerve too, and the elbow segment is not involved.

questions.q: In a milder case with normal routine values, which extra study is commonly added to look for subtle median slowing at the wrist?
options: A median-ulnar comparison over the same distance (for example to digit 4)
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the abductor digiti minimi
A sural sensory study on the same side
A blink reflex study on the symptomatic side
questions.explanation: Comparison studies (median versus ulnar to digit 4, median versus radial to the thumb, or palmar mixed comparisons) measure two nerves over the same distance in the same hand, so a small median delay stands out. This app's reference lists a difference of 0.5 ms or more as abnormal. RNS, sural and blink reflex studies answer different questions.

cases.title: Little finger numbness and a weak grip
cases.referral: 61M, R numbness little finger and ulnar half of ring finger, weak grip, leans on elbows at work. NCS R arm, r/o ulnar neuropathy at the elbow.
cases.why: Suspected ulnar neuropathy needs ulnar motor studies with stimulation below and above the elbow (elbow flexed), an ulnar sensory study, and median studies to show the problem is confined to the ulnar nerve.

questions.q: Where along the ulnar nerve is the abnormality?
options: Across the elbow, with slowing and an amplitude drop above the elbow
At the wrist, with a prolonged distal motor latency
Throughout the forearm, with uniform slowing in every segment
In the median nerve, with ulnar studies within limits
questions.explanation: The wrist and below-elbow responses are normal, but the above-elbow response is smaller and the across-elbow velocity is slow compared with the forearm. That localizes the slowing and partial block to the elbow segment. The distal latency is normal and the median studies are normal.

questions.q: Why must the elbow be flexed when you stimulate and measure across it?
options: So the tape measures the true nerve length and the velocity is not falsely slow
So the nerve moves away from the stimulator and needs less current
So the hand muscles relax and the CMAP becomes larger
So the ground electrode makes better contact with the skin
questions.explanation: With the elbow straight the ulnar nerve lies slack in the groove, so the skin measurement underestimates the nerve length and the calculated across-elbow velocity looks slower than it is. Flexing the elbow (about 70 to 90 degrees) takes up the slack, so the surface distance matches the nerve. Flexion does not reduce the current needed, enlarge the CMAP or change ground contact.

cases.title: A cold hand on a winter morning
cases.referral: 28F, intermittent tingling both hands, normal exam. Arrived from outside. NCS R arm, r/o CTS.
cases.why: Median motor and sensory studies with an ulnar sensory comparison answer the CTS question. The trap in this case is temperature: measure it first.

questions.q: If you had recorded this hand without warming it, how would the results have misled the reader?
options: Prolonged latencies and slow velocities that mimic a neuropathy
Low amplitudes that mimic axonal loss in every nerve
Absent responses that mimic a complete nerve injury
Faster velocities that hide a real demyelinating neuropathy
questions.explanation: Cooling slows conduction: latencies lengthen and velocities fall, while amplitudes tend to rise. A cold hand can therefore make a healthy median nerve look like carpal tunnel syndrome or a neuropathy. It does not abolish responses or speed conduction up.

questions.q: What is the best way to deal with the low temperature?
options: Warm the limb to the lab's target and recheck the temperature before recording
Record now and apply a correction factor without measuring the temperature
Increase the current to 100 mA so that the responses are supramaximal
Lower the high filter to 500 Hz so that the slower responses look sharper
questions.explanation: Warming (warm packs, a heating lamp or warm water per lab policy) to at least the lab target, about 32 °C in the hand in this app, and rechecking is the preferred approach. Correction factors are a fallback some labs use only with a documented temperature. Raising the current or changing filters does not correct for temperature.

cases.title: Burning feet in diabetes
cases.referral: 67M, T2DM x15 yr, burning feet, reduced ankle jerks. NCS R leg, r/o polyneuropathy.
cases.why: A length-dependent polyneuropathy is screened in the longest nerves first: sural sensory, fibular and tibial motor studies in the leg. Arm studies are often added to show the gradient and exclude a superimposed entrapment.

questions.q: Which description fits these leg results best?
options: Low sensory and motor amplitudes with mildly reduced velocities
Markedly slow velocities with conduction block in every nerve
Normal sensory responses with low motor amplitudes only
Focal slowing confined to the segment across the fibular head
questions.explanation: The sural SNAP and the fibular and tibial CMAPs are small while velocities are only mildly reduced, the pattern of a length-dependent axonal sensorimotor polyneuropathy. Demyelination would give marked slowing and block, normal SNAPs would point away from a neuropathy, and there is no focal change at the fibular head.

questions.q: The sural response is only a few microvolts. Which step helps you record and measure it reliably?
options: Average several sweeps and confirm the electrode placement
Set the gain to 200 µV per division so it looks cleaner
Raise the low filter to 200 Hz to remove the baseline drift
Move G1 to the medial malleolus where the nerve is larger
questions.explanation: Averaging reduces random noise while the time-locked response stays, and checking G1 behind the lateral malleolus and G2 distal along the foot rules out a placement error. A gain of 200 µV per division would make a small SNAP almost flat, a 200 Hz low filter would shrink it further, and the sural nerve runs behind the lateral, not medial, malleolus.

cases.title: Ascending weakness after a stomach bug
cases.referral: 45F, 9 days of ascending weakness and tingling after a diarrhoeal illness, areflexia. NCS, r/o GBS (AIDP).
cases.why: Suspected Guillain-Barre syndrome needs several motor nerves with proximal stimulation (to look for slowing, conduction block and dispersion) and sensory studies in the arm and leg (to look for sural sparing).

questions.q: Which features of the motor studies point toward demyelination?
options: Prolonged distal latencies, slow velocities, conduction block and dispersion
Low amplitudes with normal latencies and normal velocities
Normal motor studies with absent sensory responses only
A decrement of the response during repeated stimulation
questions.explanation: Demyelination slows conduction (long distal latencies, slow velocities), makes some fibres fail to conduct (conduction block) and spreads out arrival times (temporal dispersion). Pure low amplitudes suggest axonal loss, and a decrement on repetitive stimulation is a neuromuscular junction finding.

questions.q: The median sensory response is absent while the sural response is normal. What is this called?
options: Sural sparing, often seen in acquired demyelinating neuropathy
A length-dependent pattern of a diabetic axonal neuropathy
A technical failure of the sural recording that should be redone
A sign that the lesion is proximal to the dorsal root ganglion
questions.explanation: An abnormal arm SNAP with a normal sural SNAP is the reverse of the length-dependent pattern and is called sural sparing, a supportive finding in Guillain-Barre syndrome. A length-dependent neuropathy affects the sural nerve first. A preganglionic lesion would leave the SNAPs normal.

questions.q: Why did you need more current than usual to reach a maximal response?
options: Demyelinated nerves can have raised stimulation thresholds
The ground electrode was placed on the wrong limb
The high filter setting raises the current that is needed
Supramaximal current is lower in warm limbs than in cold ones
questions.explanation: Demyelinated or swollen nerves can need more current to excite every axon, so keep raising the current until the response stops growing before calling a response low. The ground and filter settings do not change the threshold.

cases.title: Foot drop after weight loss
cases.referral: 38M, R foot drop 3 wk after losing 15 kg, crosses legs at work, numb dorsum of foot. NCS R leg.
cases.why: Foot drop needs fibular motor studies with stimulation below and above the fibular head, plus a tibial motor and a sural study to show whether nerves outside the fibular territory are involved.

questions.q: Where is the conduction abnormality?
options: Across the fibular head, between the below-head and popliteal sites
At the ankle, with a prolonged distal motor latency
In the tibial nerve, with the fibular nerve within limits
In the sural nerve, with the motor studies within limits
questions.explanation: The ankle and below-fibular-head responses are normal but the popliteal response is much smaller and the across-knee velocity is slow, so the block and slowing sit at the fibular head, a common compression site with weight loss and leg crossing. The tibial and sural studies are normal.

questions.q: Which sensory study tests the sensory branch of the same nerve?
options: Superficial fibular sensory study
Sural sensory study
Saphenous sensory study
Medial plantar sensory study
questions.explanation: The superficial fibular (peroneal) nerve is a branch of the common fibular nerve and supplies the dorsum of the foot. The sural nerve comes mainly from the tibial nerve (medial sural cutaneous), often joined by a communicating branch of the common fibular nerve, so it is not a direct test of the fibular sensory fibres. The saphenous nerve is a branch of the femoral nerve, and the medial plantar nerve is a branch of the tibial nerve.

cases.title: A CMAP with a positive dip
cases.referral: 30F, healthy volunteer for a technique check. A colleague set up the median motor study; the response starts with a small positive dip.
cases.why: Only the median motor study is needed. The task is to find and fix the set-up problem.

questions.q: What was causing the initial positive deflection?
options: G1 was not over the motor point of the muscle
The stimulation was already supramaximal
The low filter was set at 10 Hz
The hand was warmer than 32 °C
questions.explanation: A CMAP should start with a sharp negative takeoff when G1 sits over the motor point. If G1 is off the motor point, the response is first seen at a distance as a positive deflection. Supramaximal current, a 10 Hz low filter and a warm hand do not cause it.

questions.q: With G1 correctly placed, an initial positive dip appears only when the median nerve is stimulated at the elbow. What is a classic cause?
options: A median-to-ulnar (Martin-Gruber) anastomosis in the forearm
Carpal tunnel syndrome slowing the distal median segment
A cold hand slowing conduction in the median nerve
A loose ground electrode on the back of the hand
questions.explanation: In a Martin-Gruber anastomosis some median-nerve fibres cross to the ulnar nerve in the forearm. Elbow stimulation then also activates ulnar-innervated hand muscles, whose volume-conducted response reaches the APB electrode as a positive dip, especially when carpal tunnel syndrome slows the median fibres. A cold hand or a loose ground does not give a positive dip at one site only.

cases.title: Neck pain and a numb thumb
cases.referral: 50M, neck pain radiating to the R thumb, numb thumb, weak elbow flexion. NCS R arm, CTS vs C6 radiculopathy.
cases.why: Thumb numbness can come from the median nerve at the wrist, the superficial radial nerve or the C6 root. Median motor and sensory and superficial radial sensory studies separate a nerve lesion from a root lesion.

questions.q: Median and superficial radial sensory responses are normal although the thumb is numb. What does that suggest?
options: A lesion proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, such as a root lesion
Carpal tunnel syndrome affecting the median nerve at the wrist
A brachial plexus lesion distal to the dorsal root ganglion
A radial nerve lesion at the spiral groove of the humerus
questions.explanation: The dorsal root ganglion lies in the intervertebral foramen, outside the dura. A root lesion is proximal to it, so the sensory axons from the ganglion to the skin stay intact and the SNAPs stay normal even though the patient feels numb. Carpal tunnel syndrome, plexus lesions and radial nerve lesions damage those axons and lower the SNAPs.

questions.q: Which test does the physician usually add to look for a radiculopathy?
options: Needle EMG including the paraspinal muscles
Repetitive nerve stimulation of the hand
A blink reflex study on the same side
A sural sensory study on the same side
questions.explanation: Needle EMG of muscles in the C6 myotome, including the paraspinals, looks for denervation in a root pattern. Repetitive stimulation tests the neuromuscular junction, the blink reflex tests the trigeminal and facial pathways, and the sural nerve is in the leg.

cases.title: A wasted thumb muscle
cases.referral: 71F, years of numb R thumb/index/middle, now drops cups; thenar wasting on exam. NCS R arm, r/o severe CTS.
cases.why: Median motor and sensory studies answer the question, and ulnar motor and sensory studies in the same hand show whether the problem is confined to the median nerve.

questions.q: The median SNAP is not seen at the standard settings. What should you do before recording it as absent?
options: Report it as absent straight away, since the patient has wasting
Increase the sensitivity, average several sweeps, and confirm placement and supramaximal stimulation
Switch to a 500 Hz high filter so the response becomes broader and easier to see
Move the recording rings to the little finger and record from there instead
questions.explanation: An absent response is a strong finding, so make sure it is real: raise the sensitivity (for example 10 µV/division), average sweeps to lift a tiny response out of the noise, check the ring positions and skin, and make sure the current is supramaximal. A 500 Hz high filter distorts and shrinks a SNAP, and the little finger is ulnar territory.

questions.q: What pattern do the results show?
options: A normal study with a technical problem in the median sensory set-up
Diffuse demyelinating polyneuropathy affecting both median and ulnar nerves
Ulnar neuropathy at the wrist with secondary median involvement
Severe median abnormality at the wrist: absent SNAP, long distal motor latency and a low CMAP, with normal ulnar studies
questions.explanation: The median distal motor latency is markedly prolonged and the thenar CMAP is small, the median SNAP is absent, and the ulnar studies in the same hand are normal. That is severe focal median involvement at the wrist with axonal loss (the small CMAP and the wasting). Interpreting and grading severity belongs to the physician; EMG of the abductor pollicis brevis is often added.

cases.title: Tingling fingers, borderline numbers
cases.referral: 39F, data entry clerk, intermittent R index/middle tingling for 3 months, normal exam. NCS R arm, r/o early CTS.
cases.why: Early carpal tunnel syndrome first slows the median sensory fibres across the wrist. Median sensory (wrist and palm), median motor and an ulnar sensory study in the same hand give the comparison you need.

questions.q: Record the median sensory response from the wrist (14 cm) and from the palm (7 cm). Which segment shows the slowing?
options: The palm-to-digit segment, which is slow as well as the wrist
Neither: both latencies are well inside the reference limits
The wrist-to-palm segment across the carpal tunnel, while palm-to-digit is normal
The forearm segment above the wrist, proximal to the stimulation site
questions.explanation: The palm peak latency is normal (about 1.8 ms), so the nerve from the palm to the finger conducts normally. The wrist response takes about 1.8 ms longer than the palm response for its extra 7 cm, where a healthy hand needs about 1.3 ms, so the delay sits in the 7 cm between wrist and palm, across the carpal tunnel. Splitting the nerve into segments like this localizes slowing that a single wrist-to-digit study can only hint at.

questions.q: Why is the palm study useful when routine values are only borderline?
options: It replaces the need for the ulnar sensory study in the same hand
It isolates the short segment across the carpal tunnel, where early slowing is concentrated
It removes the effect of a cold hand, so temperature no longer matters
It measures motor fibres, which are affected before sensory fibres in CTS
questions.explanation: Slowing confined to a few centimetres is diluted over a 14 cm wrist-to-digit study. The palm site lets you compare the palm-to-digit and wrist-to-palm halves directly, so focal slowing across the wrist stands out. Temperature still matters, sensory fibres are usually affected first, and the ulnar comparison is still needed.

questions.q: The median wrist peak latency is about 3.6 ms and the ulnar wrist peak latency, over the same 14 cm, is about 3.1 ms. How is that difference usually judged?
options: Not significant, because both values are under the 4.0 ms limit
Significant only if the median amplitude is also low
Not comparable, because the median and ulnar nerves always differ by about 1 ms
Abnormal: a median-ulnar difference of about 0.5 ms or more over the same distance supports focal median slowing
questions.explanation: Each value alone is within the reference limit, but the two nerves were tested in the same hand, at the same temperature, over the same distance. In this app's reference a median-ulnar difference of 0.5 ms or more is abnormal, so a difference of about 0.5 ms supports early median slowing at the wrist. Amplitude can still be normal in early CTS; your lab's comparison cut-offs take precedence.

cases.title: A long-distance cyclist with a weak hand
cases.referral: 34M, cycles 300 km a week on drop handlebars; 6 weeks of R hand weakness and clumsiness, no numbness. NCS R arm.
cases.why: Hand weakness in the ulnar distribution needs ulnar motor studies at the wrist, below and above the elbow, the ulnar SNAP, and median studies to show the problem is confined to the ulnar nerve.

questions.q: Where do the ulnar results place the problem?
options: Distal to the wrist, in motor fibres: long distal latency and low CMAP at every site, normal velocities, normal ulnar SNAP
Across the elbow: slowing and a drop in amplitude between below- and above-elbow sites
In the C8 root: normal motor studies and an absent ulnar SNAP
In a polyneuropathy: all four nerves are equally abnormal
questions.explanation: Every ulnar motor response is small and the distal latency is prolonged, but the forearm and across-elbow velocities are normal and there is no extra drop across the elbow, so the abnormality lies distal to the wrist stimulation site. The ulnar SNAP is normal, so the sensory fibres to the little finger are spared. That fits compression of the motor branch at the wrist or palm (Guyon's canal), common with handlebar pressure.

questions.q: Which sensory study helps separate an ulnar lesion at the wrist from one at the elbow?
options: The median sensory response to the index finger
The sural sensory response on the same side
The dorsal ulnar cutaneous sensory response, which branches off above the wrist
The superficial radial sensory response at the snuffbox
questions.explanation: The dorsal ulnar cutaneous branch leaves the ulnar nerve in the forearm, above Guyon's canal. It is spared by lesions at the wrist but often abnormal with lesions at the elbow. Median, radial and sural responses come from other nerves.

cases.title: A burning sole after an ankle fracture
cases.referral: 48F, R medial ankle fracture last year; now burning and numbness of the R sole, worse when standing. NCS R leg, r/o tarsal tunnel.
cases.why: The tibial motor study to the abductor hallucis crosses the tarsal tunnel. The fibular motor and sural studies on the same leg show whether the problem is confined to the tibial nerve at the ankle or part of a wider neuropathy.

questions.q: What pattern do your results show?
options: A length-dependent polyneuropathy affecting all three nerves
Fibular neuropathy at the fibular head
Focal tibial abnormality at the ankle: prolonged distal latency and small AH response, with normal fibular and sural studies
Normal studies, because the popliteal-to-ankle velocity is normal
questions.explanation: The tibial distal motor latency to the abductor hallucis is prolonged and the response is small, while the tibial velocity from knee to ankle is normal and the fibular and sural studies are normal. The abnormality is in the short segment from the ankle stimulation site to the foot, where the nerve runs through the tarsal tunnel. A normal proximal velocity does not exclude a distal lesion.

questions.q: Which additional studies are commonly added for suspected tarsal tunnel syndrome?
options: Medial and lateral plantar sensory or mixed studies, compared with the other foot
Repetitive stimulation of the abductor hallucis at 3 Hz
Median and ulnar F-waves in both arms
Blink reflexes and facial motor studies
questions.explanation: The medial and lateral plantar nerves are the terminal branches of the tibial nerve beyond the tarsal tunnel; their sensory or mixed responses, compared side to side, are more sensitive than the motor study. Plantar responses can be small even in healthy older adults, so the comparison with the asymptomatic foot matters.

cases.title: High arches and a family history
cases.referral: 24M, lifelong clumsy running, high arches and hammer toes; father and aunt similar. NCS R arm and leg.
cases.why: A suspected inherited neuropathy needs motor studies with proximal and distal sites in arm and leg (to judge whether slowing is uniform) and sensory studies in arm and leg.

questions.q: How would you describe the conduction velocities?
options: Normal in the arm and slow only in the leg
Slow only across the elbow and the fibular head
Uniformly and markedly slow in every nerve and segment, with no conduction block or temporal dispersion
Normal everywhere, with only low amplitudes
questions.explanation: Velocities are less than half of normal (in the low 20s m/s) in every nerve and every segment, and the proximal responses are similar in shape and size to the distal ones: no conduction block, no excess dispersion. Uniform slowing like this is typical of an inherited demyelinating neuropathy such as Charcot-Marie-Tooth type 1A, because every myelinated fibre is affected in the same way.

questions.q: Which feature would instead point toward an acquired demyelinating neuropathy such as CIDP?
options: Conduction block and temporal dispersion at sites that are not usual compression points
Velocities that are equally slow in every nerve
High arches and a positive family history
Absent sural responses
questions.explanation: Acquired demyelination is patchy: some segments are slowed more than others, and conduction block or excess temporal dispersion appears at non-compression sites. Inherited demyelination is uniform. High arches and a family history support an inherited cause; absent SNAPs occur in both.

cases.title: Weak in a week, but no numbness
cases.referral: 19M, 6 days of rapidly ascending weakness after a diarrhoeal illness; no sensory symptoms, areflexia. NCS, r/o GBS.
cases.why: Suspected Guillain-Barré syndrome needs motor studies with proximal sites in arm and leg and sensory studies in arm and leg, to decide whether the process is demyelinating or axonal and whether sensory fibres are involved.

questions.q: Which pattern fits your results?
options: Demyelinating GBS (AIDP): long latencies, slow velocities and dispersion
Low motor amplitudes with normal latencies and velocities, and normal sensory responses
Length-dependent sensory axonal polyneuropathy
Normal motor and sensory studies
questions.explanation: Every motor response is small, but distal latencies and velocities are normal and there is no dispersion, while median and sural SNAPs are normal. That pure motor axonal pattern fits the acute motor axonal neuropathy (AMAN) form of GBS, which often follows Campylobacter infection. AIDP would show demyelinating features.

questions.q: Why may the reader ask for a repeat study in 1 to 2 weeks?
options: Because AMAN never shows abnormalities on the first study
Because the low amplitudes may be a technical error that time will correct
To measure whether the fever has affected limb temperature
Because early reversible conduction failure and evolving changes can change the classification
questions.explanation: In early GBS the findings evolve. Some axonal-looking patients have reversible conduction failure at the nodes and recover amplitude quickly, while others show more axonal loss. Serial studies help classify the subtype and follow recovery. Technical checks belong in the first study, not in a repeat.

cases.title: Weak legs, dry mouth, a long smoking history
cases.referral: 62M, 40 pack-years, 4 months of difficulty climbing stairs, dry mouth; reflexes reduced but improve after brief effort. NCS R arm and leg.
cases.why: Proximal weakness with reduced reflexes needs motor and sensory studies first, to see whether nerves, the neuromuscular junction or muscle is the likely level.

questions.q: The CMAPs are small everywhere with normal latencies and velocities, and the SNAPs are normal. Which quick test should you be ready to add at the reader's request?
options: A second sural sensory study on the other leg
Repeat the ADM response immediately after 10 seconds of maximal voluntary contraction
Lower the high filter to 1 kHz and repeat each motor study
Stimulate the ulnar nerve at the axilla to look for a proximal block
questions.explanation: Small resting CMAPs with normal sensory responses raise the possibility of a presynaptic neuromuscular junction disorder such as Lambert-Eaton myasthenic syndrome. After 10 seconds of maximal exercise the CMAP amplitude increases markedly; an increase of about 100% or more strongly suggests LEMS. Repetitive stimulation (decrement at 3 Hz, increment at high rates) is the formal test.

questions.q: Which group of conditions fits low CMAPs with normal SNAPs?
options: Motor neuron disease, motor radiculopathy, motor neuropathy, NMJ disorders and some myopathies
Carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy at the elbow
Sensory neuronopathy and small-fibre neuropathy
A cold limb or submaximal stimulation, and nothing else
questions.explanation: SNAPs stay normal whenever the lesion spares the sensory fibres beyond the dorsal root ganglion. Low CMAPs then point to the anterior horn cell, motor roots, motor axons, the neuromuscular junction or muscle. The pattern narrows the list; EMG, exercise testing and repetitive stimulation take it further. Technical causes must be excluded first but do not explain a consistent pattern.

cases.title: A thin hand and muscle twitching
cases.referral: 58M, 8 months of R hand weakness, visible twitching in both arms, no numbness; brisk reflexes. NCS R arm and leg.
cases.why: Progressive weakness without sensory loss needs motor studies with proximal sites (to exclude conduction block) and sensory studies (to show the sensory fibres are spared), in more than one limb.

questions.q: The median (APB) response is much smaller than the ulnar (ADM) response. What is this pattern called?
options: Martin-Gruber anastomosis
Conduction block of the median nerve
Sural sparing
The split hand: the thenar side wasted more than the hypothenar side
questions.explanation: In motor neuron disease the thenar muscles (APB, first dorsal interosseous) are often more affected than the hypothenar muscles, although they share the C8-T1 roots: the 'split hand'. On NCS it shows as a disproportionately small median (APB) CMAP compared with the ulnar (ADM) CMAP, with normal SNAPs.

questions.q: Why do you stimulate the motor nerves at proximal sites for this referral?
options: To look for conduction block outside compression sites, which suggests multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable mimic
To measure the sural nerve indirectly through the leg
Because distal stimulation is not reliable in thin patients
To produce F-waves, which replace the need for EMG
questions.explanation: Multifocal motor neuropathy can look like motor neuron disease clinically, but it shows motor conduction block in segments that are not usual compression sites, and it responds to immunoglobulin treatment. Normal proximal responses without block, with normal SNAPs, fit a motor neuron disorder; EMG is needed to show widespread denervation.

cases.title: Numb hands, unsteady in the dark
cases.referral: 55F, dry eyes and dry mouth, 6 months of numb hands and face, unsteady with eyes closed; strength normal. NCS R arm and leg.
cases.why: Sensory loss needs sensory studies in the arm (median, ulnar, radial) and leg (sural), with motor studies to show whether motor fibres are involved.

questions.q: Compare the arm and leg sensory responses. What pattern do you see?
options: Length-dependent: sural absent, arm responses normal
Non-length-dependent: arm SNAPs (including radial) absent or very low, sural relatively preserved, motor studies normal
Focal median abnormality at the wrist only
Pure motor involvement with normal sensory responses
questions.explanation: In a length-dependent axonal neuropathy the longest nerves (sural) fail first. Here the arm SNAPs, including the short superficial radial nerve, are worse than the sural, and motor studies are normal. That non-length-dependent, pure sensory pattern points to the dorsal root ganglion cell bodies: a sensory neuronopathy (ganglionopathy), as seen with Sjögren syndrome, paraneoplastic syndromes or some toxins.

questions.q: Why is the radial sensory study particularly useful here?
options: It is a short nerve rarely trapped, so a very low radial SNAP argues against length dependence or entrapment
It replaces the need for the sural study
It tests motor fibres to the thumb extensors
It is the only sensory study unaffected by temperature
questions.explanation: The superficial radial nerve is short and seldom compressed. If it is very low while the much longer sural is still present, the pattern cannot be explained by length dependence or by entrapment of the median and ulnar nerves, which supports a ganglionopathy. It is a purely sensory nerve, and temperature affects it like any other.

cases.title: A thin hand and a cervical rib
cases.referral: 27F, 2 years of R hand weakness and aching inner forearm; thenar wasting; cervical rib on X-ray. NCS R arm.
cases.why: Hand weakness and wasting with ulnar-side sensory symptoms need median and ulnar motor and sensory studies, so a lower brachial plexus lesion can be separated from carpal tunnel syndrome and ulnar neuropathy.

questions.q: Which pattern do your results show?
options: Carpal tunnel syndrome: slow median latencies with a normal ulnar SNAP
Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow: slowing across the elbow
Lower trunk plexus pattern: low median (APB) CMAP and low ulnar SNAP, normal median SNAP and normal latencies
C6 radiculopathy: normal sensory studies with a low radial SNAP
questions.explanation: The thenar (APB) CMAP is small though the median latency is normal, and the ulnar SNAP is low while the median SNAP (C6-C7 fibres through the upper and middle trunks) is normal. APB motor fibres (C8-T1) and the ulnar sensory fibres both run through the lower trunk, so this combination points to the lower trunk of the brachial plexus, as in true neurogenic thoracic outlet syndrome with a cervical rib or band.

questions.q: Which extra sensory study supports a lower trunk or medial cord lesion?
options: The sural sensory response
The medial antebrachial cutaneous (MABC) sensory response, compared with the other arm
The superficial radial sensory response
The median sensory response from the palm
questions.explanation: The medial antebrachial cutaneous nerve carries T1 (and C8) sensory fibres from the lower trunk and medial cord and supplies the inner forearm. A low MABC SNAP compared with the other side supports a lower plexus lesion; it is normal in ulnar neuropathy at the elbow and in C8 radiculopathy.

cases.title: Numb back of the thumb after handcuffs
cases.referral: 30M, numbness and tingling over the back of the R thumb and first web space since being handcuffed 3 weeks ago; strength normal. NCS R arm.
cases.why: Numbness on the back of the thumb is in superficial radial territory. The radial sensory study answers the question, and a median sensory study in the same hand checks that the problem is not more widespread.

questions.q: What do the results show?
options: A low superficial radial SNAP with normal median sensory responses
Absent median and radial SNAPs, as in a polyneuropathy
Prolonged median sensory latency, as in carpal tunnel syndrome
A normal radial SNAP, which excludes a nerve injury
questions.explanation: The superficial radial SNAP is low while the median sensory response is normal. An isolated low radial SNAP fits a lesion of the superficial radial nerve, which lies just under the skin at the wrist and is easily compressed by handcuffs, tight watch straps or casts (cheiralgia paresthetica).

questions.q: In a similar patient the radial SNAP is in the low-normal range. Which comparison helps most?
options: The sural response on the same side
The ulnar motor response at the wrist
The same radial study on the asymptomatic side
A median motor study at the elbow
questions.explanation: Normal ranges are wide. A side-to-side comparison of the same nerve over the same distance is more sensitive: an amplitude less than about half that of the other side is commonly treated as significant. Sural, ulnar motor and median motor studies do not test the superficial radial nerve.

cases.title: Foot drop with back pain
cases.referral: 52M, 5 weeks of R foot drop after lifting; back pain radiating down the lateral leg. NCS R leg, fibular neuropathy vs L5 radiculopathy.
cases.why: Foot drop needs the fibular motor study with stimulation below and above the fibular head (to look for a focal lesion there), plus tibial motor and sural studies on the same leg.

questions.q: The EDB response is low at the ankle, below the fibular head and at the popliteal fossa, with no drop or slowing across the fibular head. What does this tell you?
options: It proves a fibular neuropathy at the fibular head
There is axonal loss in fibular fibres, but NCS alone cannot say where: fibular nerve, sciatic nerve or L5 root
It proves an L5 radiculopathy, because the sural is normal
The study is technically invalid and must be repeated
questions.explanation: A low CMAP at every site without focal slowing or block means axonal loss somewhere proximal to the ankle, but motor NCS cannot show where the axons were damaged. A demyelinating lesion at the fibular head would show slowing or block across it. EMG (including muscles supplied by L5 but not by the fibular nerve, and the paraspinals) is needed to localize.

questions.q: Which sensory study helps separate an L5 root lesion from a fibular nerve lesion?
options: The superficial fibular sensory response: normal in L5 radiculopathy, often low in fibular nerve lesions
The median sensory response to the index finger
The sural response, which is always absent in L5 radiculopathy
The radial sensory response at the snuffbox
questions.explanation: Root lesions are proximal to the dorsal root ganglion, so the SNAP of the matching sensory nerve stays normal even with numbness. The superficial fibular nerve carries mostly L5 fibres; it is often low with fibular nerve or sciatic lesions but normal with an L5 root lesion. The sural is mainly S1 and is normal in both; median and radial responses come from the arm.

cases.title: Diabetes and night-time hand numbness
cases.referral: 64F, T2DM x12 yr with numb feet; now R thumb/index/middle numbness that wakes her at night. NCS R arm and leg.
cases.why: Two questions need answering: is there a polyneuropathy (sural and fibular studies), and is there carpal tunnel syndrome on top of it (median studies compared with ulnar studies in the same hand)?

questions.q: What do your results show?
options: A polyneuropathy alone, which explains the hand symptoms
Carpal tunnel syndrome alone, with normal leg studies
Ulnar neuropathy at the elbow with a normal leg
A length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy plus a median abnormality at the wrist out of proportion to the ulnar studies
questions.explanation: The sural SNAP is low and the fibular CMAP small: a length-dependent axonal polyneuropathy. In the arm, the median latencies are clearly prolonged while the ulnar studies in the same hand are near normal. A polyneuropathy would affect median and ulnar nerves similarly, so the disproportionate median slowing at the wrist suggests superimposed carpal tunnel syndrome.

questions.q: Why is the ulnar comparison essential in a patient with a polyneuropathy?
options: Because the ulnar nerve is never affected by diabetes
Because a polyneuropathy can slow the median nerve on its own; only a disproportionate median abnormality supports CTS
Because ulnar studies are required by every insurance protocol
Because ulnar studies show the severity of the polyneuropathy better than the sural
questions.explanation: A diffuse neuropathy can prolong median latencies by itself. Carpal tunnel syndrome is supported when the median is clearly worse than another nerve in the same hand (or than its own palm segment), not just abnormal. Diabetes can affect the ulnar nerve too, which is why the comparison is relative.

cases.title: A weak hand, no numbness, slowly worse
cases.referral: 41M, 18 months of slowly worsening R hand weakness (finger spreading, grip), no sensory symptoms, little wasting. NCS R arm.
cases.why: Weakness in ulnar-supplied hand muscles needs ulnar motor studies at the wrist, below and above the elbow, plus the ulnar SNAP and median studies for comparison.

questions.q: Where is the abnormality in the ulnar motor study?
options: Across the elbow: the amplitude drops only between below- and above-elbow sites
In the forearm: the CMAP drops by more than half between the wrist and below-elbow sites, with a normal ulnar SNAP
At the wrist: the distal latency is long and every response is small
Nowhere: all ulnar values are within limits
questions.explanation: The wrist response is normal, but stimulating below the elbow gives a much smaller response without much change in duration: conduction block in the forearm segment, which is not a usual compression site. The ulnar SNAP is normal. Motor conduction block at a non-entrapment site with normal sensory responses is the hallmark of multifocal motor neuropathy, a treatable condition.

questions.q: When is an amplitude drop between two sites usually accepted as conduction block rather than normal loss?
options: Any drop of more than 5%
Only when the distal latency is also prolonged
A large drop (for example 50% or more in arm nerves) without excessive temporal dispersion
Only when the drop is in the leg
questions.explanation: Some fall in amplitude over a long segment is normal, especially in the legs. A large proximal-to-distal drop (commonly 50% or more for definite block in arm nerves) with little increase in response duration means impulses are failing to pass. If the response is also much longer and more dispersed, phase cancellation may explain part of the drop.
